summary: Describes high-level requirements for a client-server protocol that registrars use to register and manage Internet domain names in shared registries. It focuses on basic functions and interfaces to support different registry and registrar models, not on technical protocol details.

plainLanguage.summary: Domain names are sold by shops that all share one big record book. This document lists what the shared ordering system must be able to do.

questions: what are the requirements for a registry registrar protocol
how do registrars manage domains in shared registries
what is a thick registry vs thin registry
subtitle: High-level functional requirements for domain name registration systems.

tldr.problem: Domain name registration systems need a common protocol to allow registrars to work with shared registries, reducing operational complexity and supporting multiple business models.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies high-level functional requirements that a registry-registrar protocol must support, including session management, authentication, object management, and domain status tracking.
tldr.outcome: These requirements guided the design of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), which standardized how registrars interact with domain registries.

today: RFC 3375 is an Informational document that helped establish the requirements for standardized registry-registrar protocols. The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) was subsequently developed to implement these requirements and is now the standard protocol used for domain name registry operations worldwide.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The growth of shared domain name registration systems created a need for a standard protocol that registrars could use to interact with registries. Rather than each registry defining its own protocol, a single generic protocol would let registrars communicate with multiple registries through the same interface.

This document does not propose a specific protocol design. Instead, it defines the high-level functional and interface requirements that any protocol for registry-registrar communication should support.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each record keeper having its own rules, a generic system would let all the shops talk to any record keeper in the same way.

sections.title: Domain Registration System Architecture
sections.content:
A domain name registration system involves three parties: registrants (who register domain names), registrars (who provide front-end registration services), and registries (who manage the authoritative central database and publish zone files).

Registries may be shared among multiple competing registrars, serving thousands of registrations, or dedicated to a single registrar. The protocol must support both thick registries that store all information (technical and administrative) and thin registries that distribute social information (contact details) between the registry and registrars.
sections.plainLanguage: The system has three kinds of people: customers who want a name, shops that sell the names, and the big record book that keeps the master list.

sections.title: Core Protocol Functions
sections.content:
A registry-registrar protocol must support session management to establish and end connections with version negotiation, and identification and authentication so both client and server confirm each other's identity before performing any operations.

The protocol must enable object management for domains, name servers, and social information (contact details). It must support creation, updates, queries, transfers between registrars, renewals, and deletions. Each operation must be associated with a unique transaction identifier for tracking and auditing.
sections.plainLanguage: The system needs to let shops log in securely, then create or change domain records, look them up, move them to different shops, or delete them.

sections.title: Object Management Requirements
sections.content:
Domain registration requires managing multiple object types. Domain objects must support flexible registration periods negotiated between registrar and registrant, with awareness of validity periods and automatic renewal or expiration handling. Name server objects must be registerable with IPv4 or IPv6 addresses (glue records for delegation), and must support associations with multiple domains and multiple IP addresses.

Social information objects (contact details) must be stored independently and associated with domains as registrants, technical contacts, billing contacts, or administrative contacts. These objects may be referenced by multiple registrars and registries, requiring support for shared resource references and access controls based on sponsoring registrar.
sections.plainLanguage: The system tracks three types of things: domain names (with expiration dates), name servers (with IP addresses), and contact information (names and addresses).

sections.title: Domain Status and Transaction Handling
sections.content:
Domains must support multiple status indicators reflecting their operational state. These include: newly created (registered but not yet in zone files), active (published and modifiable), inactive (modifiable but not published due to missing name servers), hold (not modifiable, not published), lock (not modifiable, published), and transfer pending. Status flags may be set independently by both registry and registrar for certain states like hold and lock.

Every transaction must report success or failure unambiguously. The protocol must provide transaction identification for record-keeping and must ensure transactional atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability even if sessions fail.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain can be in different states: newly made, active, inactive, on hold, locked, or waiting to be transferred. The system must clearly report whether each action succeeded or failed.

sections.title: Design Principles and Constraints
sections.content:
The protocol must work over IETF-approved reliable transports like TCP that include congestion control, ensuring network-friendly behavior. It must be hardware-independent, database-agnostic, and flexible enough to operate across diverse registry and registrar environments with varying governance, local laws, and business practices.

The protocol should support future extension to new object types and provide configurable optional fields controlled by registry policy, enabling sites to adapt without revising the core protocol. Security services including privacy, authentication, access control, and integrity must be available at some protocol layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The system should work over the internet, work on any computer, adapt to different countries' rules, and be easy to upgrade when new features are needed.
